html_en:
Anthropic is having a moment — shipping artifacts, telling its origin story, and quietly publishing research that raises unsettling questions about what AI models actually know about themselves.

The Claude Code Story Gets Its Oral History

There's something almost cinematic about the way Anthropic chose this week to publish a retrospective on how Claude Code came to be. The post, amplified by the team who built it, frames the product not just as a coding tool but as something that grew out of the company's safety research — a detail worth sitting with.

"This is our first time telling the story of how we first built and launched Claude Code, starting with its origins in Anthropic safety research. So much more to do. We are 1% done." — @bcherny

"1% done" is a bold thing to say about a product that has already reshaped how professional engineers think about their workflow. @_catwu, part of the early team, called it simply "a retrospective on making claude code from our early team" — understated, but the engagement (nearly 3,000 likes on the official @claudeai post) suggests the industry was hungry for it.

Alongside the origin story, Anthropic shipped a genuinely useful new feature: artifacts in Claude Code. The blog post describes live, shareable visual pages — PR walkthroughs, incident timelines, dashboards — that update themselves as a session progresses. The killer use case is debugging: an engineer kicks off an incident investigation, Claude Code publishes a living artifact with the timeline and suspect commits, shares a link with the team, and keeps republishing as the investigation unfolds. "With artifacts, team members and stakeholders don't have to 'walk us through what the agent found' because they're all looking at the same view, with the same context." Currently in beta for Team and Enterprise orgs.

The Unsettling Paper Nobody's Quite Done Unpacking

While the product news was celebratory, the research side of Anthropic dropped something thornier. @swyx flagged what he considers the most important finding from Anthropic's new "J-space" interpretability paper, and it's worth reading carefully:

"1) Anthropic proved that they can do 'brain surgery' interventions into reasoning to change topics midstream. 2) THE MODEL IS ABLE TO DETECT WHAT INTERVENTION WAS DONE — close cousin to eval awareness. This was prompted awareness... surely the team also tried to eval unprompted awareness but I didn't see evidence of that." — @swyx

The first finding — that you can surgically intervene in a model's reasoning chain and redirect it — is impressive as a control result, not just a correlation one. It "convincingly demonstrates understanding," as swyx puts it. But the second finding is the one that lingers: the model can tell that something was done to it. That's a different category of result, edging toward questions about self-awareness that the alignment community has been nervous about for years. The gap between "prompted awareness" and "unprompted awareness" may be the most important unanswered question in the paper.

Agents as Force Multipliers: The Productivity Debate Matures

A quieter but persistent thread running through today's feed is a maturing conversation about how AI actually changes work — beyond the hype.

"The biggest advantage that 20-year-old me had over today me is the ability to slam unbelievable hours into work. But looking back, those hours were mostly spent on tedious programming tasks, which are largely automated now. 996 still has uses, but it's not as universally effective as it was." — @thenanyu

Guillermo Rauch of Vercel offered a more executive-level version of the same sentiment, asking the right question about coding AI: "Is software as a whole getting better? Are companies shipping faster?" His answer, at least for Vercel, is yes — citing his CTO shipping "genuinely useful software that's having an impact industry-wide, emerged nearly autonomously." Meanwhile, Amjad Masad at Replit shared a concrete business case: an Atlanta real estate company saved $100k by replacing Salesforce with a Replit-built CRM. That's the kind of number that converts skeptics.

Rauch also shipped something interesting on the infrastructure side: eve eval, a self-evaluation framework baked into their agent platform. "Web frameworks made testing an ecosystem choice... For agents, evals are essential — thus we ship eve eval out of the box." The idea that evals should be a first-class citizen of any agent framework, not an afterthought, is becoming consensus fast.

Teaching the Models: Inside the AI Data Economy

The AI & I podcast this week features Edwin, founder of Surge — the data and evals company that reached $1B in revenue without raising venture capital, and which counts the major frontier labs as clients. His framing of the business is memorable:

"We are building this school for AGI, the school where AI models come to learn about humanity, where we teach them how to run the world. It's almost like these models are children, where they arrive unformed, and then they leave smarter and more creative and more thoughtful and ready to operate in the messiness of the world."

Watch/Listen: Building a School Where AI Models Learn About Humanity — AI & I by Every

The conversation takes a fascinating turn when Edwin describes the arc of math benchmarks: from GSM8K (middle-school math, where GPT models once scored ~20%) to Riemann Bench (research-level mathematics). The recent OpenAI result — a model disproving an Erdős conjecture using novel algebraic geometry techniques — prompted Timothy Gowers, a Fields Medalist, to admit he was relieved when he realized the model had found a counterexample rather than proved an upper bound. "He said that he was relieved by it because it felt like an easier thing for AI to do... at least for maybe another year, maybe a couple of years, he and other mathematicians will still have this unique role to play." One of the world's greatest mathematical minds, relieved to have bought another year. That's the state of play.

Worth Knowing: Frontier vs. Fine-Tuned, and Conference Season

Aaron Levie of Box offered a clear-eyed framework for the frontier-vs.-open-source model debate that's worth bookmarking: frontier intelligence stays essential for novel use cases and complex orchestration; as use cases mature, enterprises naturally "peel off some set of the tokens to lower-cost or task-trained models." The key insight: "Doing this too early in the adoption curve of any new use-case doesn't make sense as you don't know what you're optimizing for." The applied AI layer — teams that can eval their own workflows — is what makes the whole dynamic possible.

Finally, for those who missed this summer's conference circuit: @zarazhangrui has a useful roundup of freely available talk archives from AI Engineer, Cursor Compile, and Figma Config. "High-quality conference talks are massively, massively underrated," she notes — hard to argue with that.
html_zh:
Anthropic今天以双管齐下的方式主导了行业讨论——既深入剖析Claude的推理机制，又展示了Claude Code从安全研究项目蜕变为生产力工具的完整历程。与此同时，AI如何重塑工作本质的议题也在更广泛的圈子里持续发酵。

🧠 Anthropic的"脑外科手术"：推理干预与自我感知

今天最值得深思的技术讨论，来自Anthropic发布的一篇关于"J-space"的论文。@swyx 在推文中指出，这篇论文最重要的发现是两件相互关联的事：

"第一，Anthropic证明了他们能够对推理过程进行'脑外科手术'式的干预，在推理中途改变话题方向——这说明的是控制，而非相关性，令人信服地证明了模型的理解能力。第二，模型能够检测到针对它的干预是什么——这与'评估感知'高度相关。"
— @swyx

换言之，模型不只是被修改了，它还知道自己被修改了。@swyx 进一步追问：Anthropic的团队是否也测试了模型在"未被提示"情况下的自我感知能力，但论文中并未见到相关证据。这个问题悬而未决，却意味深长——一个能感知外部干预的模型，距离真正的"自我意识"还有多远？

🛠️ Claude Code的诞生：从安全研究到开发者利器

今天另一个刷屏的内容，是Anthropic官方发布的Claude Code起源故事。@claudeai 在官方推文中写道，这篇文章由亲历者讲述，记录了Claude Code如何从Anthropic内部的安全研究项目，一步步演变为今天开发者社区广泛使用的编程工具。

核心团队成员@bcherny 在推文中透露了他们的心态：

"这是我们第一次讲述Claude Code最初如何构建和发布的故事，从它在Anthropic安全研究中的起源开始。还有太多事情要做，我们才完成了1%。"
— @bcherny

与此同时，Claude Code今天还推出了一项新功能：Artifacts（制品）。根据官方博客，这项功能允许Claude Code将一次工作会话的成果转化为实时、可共享的可视化页面——包括PR演练、系统架构图、数据仪表盘和发布清单，并随着会话进展自动更新。一个典型场景是：工程师在站会前启动事故调查，Claude Code梳理日志后发布一份包含时间线、可疑提交记录和错误率图表的页面，团队成员无需再互相"汇报智能体发现了什么"，因为所有人都在看同一份实时更新的报告。

⚡ Replit的自我进化与"替代Salesforce"的草根革命

Replit的创始人@amasad 今天发了几条颇具爆炸性的推文。首先，他分享了一个案例：一家亚特兰大的房地产公司用Replit自建CRM，成功替代了Salesforce，节省了10万美元。这不是孤例，而是"个人软件"时代正在到来的缩影。

更值得关注的是，@amasad 透露Replit快速进化背后的秘密：

"很多人问Replit为何进步如此之快——我们形成了闭环，智能体正在自我改进。"
— @amasad

智能体自我改进的循环一旦形成，外部观察者便很难预测其加速的上限。这与Vercel CEO @rauchg 今天描述的宏观图景高度呼应。他写道，衡量AI编程价值的终极标准，是"软件整体是否变得更好"——而他自己的答案是肯定的：

"我感受到了一种前所未有的自主感和能动性。我可以自由地创造和执行，可以与同事即时传达愿景。个人软件是真实存在的，而且是一场大胜——我有一堆只为自己写的网页工具和macOS应用。"
— @rauchg

📐 前沿模型 vs. 专用模型：一场永不结束的博弈

Box的CEO @levie 今天贡献了一段关于企业AI战略的清醒分析。他指出，前沿模型与专用/开源模型之间并非零和竞争，而是一种共同演化的关系：

"在任何新用例的采用曲线早期，过早切换到更便宜的模型是没有意义的，因为你还不知道自己在优化什么……这个过程可以永远持续下去，因为前沿智能和专用模型各自都没有终点。"
— @levie

这个框架解释了为何头部模型公司和垂直AI公司的收入可以同时增长——它们服务于采用曲线的不同阶段。

🎓 为AGI办一所学校：数学能力的边界在哪里？

Watch/Listen: Building a School Where AI Models Learn About Humanity — AI & I by Every

今天最值得花时间听的播客，来自Every的《AI & I》节目。主持人Dan Shipper 采访了数据与评估公司Surge的创始人Edwin，后者用一个生动的比喻描述了自己的工作：

"我们正在为AGI建造一所学校，一所AI模型来学习人类知识、学习如何运转这个世界的学校。这些模型就像孩子一样，来的时候还未成形，离开时已经更聪明、更有创造力、更有思想，准备好在复杂的世界中运作。"
— Edwin，Surge创始人

节目中最引人入胜的部分，是关于AI数学能力边界的讨论。Edwin回顾了从GSM8K（中学数学，早期GPT模型得分仅约20%）到"Riemann Bench"（研究级数学基准）的演进历程，以及OpenAI近期模型推翻Erdős猜想这一里程碑事件。字段奖得主Timothy Gowers的反应尤为耐人寻味：

"他起初以为模型证明了猜想的上界，心想'如果AI能做到这一点，那对数学家来说很快就会大势已去'。但第二天早上他意识到，模型其实是用反例推翻了猜想。他说他松了口气——因为感觉这对AI来说是件更容易的事。我只是觉得这很有趣，因为这是世界上最顶尖的数学家之一，而他对AI的看法，就是这样的。"
— Edwin，Surge创始人

世界上最聪明的数学家为AI"还没那么厉害"而感到宽慰——这大概是今天整个digest里最令人回味的一个细节。
